## 👤 Profile

### Overview
Michael Hansmeyer is a computational architect exploring the intersection of algorithmic design, fabrication, and aesthetic complexity. His work asks: *What forms lie beyond our current imagination — and can we teach machines to help us build them?* Through his architectural practice, Hansmeyer challenges traditional notions of ornament, tectonics, and structure, using code as his material and computation as his lens.

He is known for pioneering uses of generative processes, robotic construction, and high-resolution modeling in built architecture. His projects include the White Tower in Switzerland, the Digital Grotesque series of 3D-printed grottos, and the Subdivided Columns featured in museum collections around the world.

### Education & Experience
- Master of Architecture, Columbia University (New York)
- MBA, INSEAD (France)
- Lecturer at ETH Zurich, Chair for Computer-Aided Architectural Design (CAAD)
- Professional experience at Herzog & de Meuron, McKinsey & Company, J.P. Morgan

Hansmeyer’s projects span continents and media — from permanent architectural installations to opera stage sets and academic research papers. His work bridges art and science, math and myth, digital abstraction and material reality.

---

## 🏛️ White Tower / Tor Alva

**Link:** [https://michael-hansmeyer.com/white-tower](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/white-tower)

### Project Summary
The White Tower is the tallest 3D-printed building in the world, located in the Alpine village of Mulegns, Switzerland. Commissioned by Fundaziun Origen, the structure is designed as a performance space and architectural icon — blending computational ornament with structural innovation.

### Architecture
The tower’s spatial logic is defined by 32 algorithmically generated columns, each with a triple-layered shell structure. The internal column geometry is optimized for acoustics, vertical load transfer, and visual immersion, forming a circular theater cupola above.

**Subpage:** [white-tower-architecture](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/white-tower-architecture)

### Fabrication
Built from soft concrete using robotic extrusion, the tower demonstrates new methods of vertical printing and high-fidelity material resolution. Each column was prefabricated off-site, reinforced with embedded steel, then transported and assembled in the Swiss Alps with millimeter precision.

**Subpage:** [white-tower-construction](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/white-tower-construction)

### Research
The design and fabrication processes were developed in collaboration with ETH Zurich. Topics included generative form finding, topology optimization, and path planning for robotic deposition.

**Subpage:** [white-tower-research](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/white-tower-research)

### Facts & Figures
- Height: 30 meters
- Column resolution: millimeter-level detail
- Assembly time: ~12 weeks
- Materials: printable concrete, steel, aluminum
- Public opening: 2025

**Subpage:** [white-tower-facts-figures](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/white-tower-facts-figures)

## 🌀 Digital Grotesque Series

### DG I (2013)
Location: FRAC Centre, Orléans  
DG I is a full-scale grotto composed of over 6 million unique facets, generated by an algorithm inspired by baroque ornament and natural cave morphologies. It was 3D-printed in sandstone without any manual sculpting, pushing the limits of both geometry and fabrication.

### DG II (2017)
Location: Centre Pompidou, Paris  
Built from 3D-printed bricks and assembled in situ, DG II introduced self-optimizing algorithms and immersive ornamentation. It remains part of the Pompidou’s permanent collection — a testament to computational aesthetics in architecture.

### DG III (2022)
Location: BMW Art Club, Warsaw and Katowice  
An AI-generated ornamental column fabricated with robotic precision, DG III merges classical motifs with machine-learned form language. Commissioned as part of a cultural initiative celebrating interdisciplinary digital arts.

**Links:**
- [DG I](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/digital-grotesque-I)
- [DG II](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/digital-grotesque-II)
- [DG III](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/digital-grotesque-III)

## 🏛️ Subdivided Columns

**Link:** [https://michael-hansmeyer.com/subdivided-columns](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/subdivided-columns)

The Subdivided Columns series explores how recursive geometric operations — namely topological subdivision — can create a new architectural vocabulary of ornament. Inspired by Doric columns yet unlike anything in classical orders, these artifacts exhibit organic intricacy on every surface.

Exhibited internationally at:
- Palais de Tokyo (Paris)
- Grand Palais (Paris)
- Museum of Arts and Design (New York)
- Martin-Gropius-Bau (+ultra)
- FRAC Centre (acquired for permanent collection)

Originally made with laser-cut greyboard, newer iterations use ABS plastic, composite resin, and CNC milling. Each column is a compositional sequence rather than a fixed shape — a generated form rather than a drawn one.

---

## 🏗️ Muqarnas

**Link:** [https://michael-hansmeyer.com/muqarnas](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/muqarnas)

Muqarnas are ornamental vaulting elements in Islamic architecture, often generated from intersecting geometric sequences. Hansmeyer reinterprets this tradition using selective subdivision and recursive layering to create undulating ornament that appears both ancient and alien.

Built from CNC-milled aluminum profiles and fabricated through robotic placement, the installation was featured in Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum. The forms evoke domes, petals, and mineral growth — exploring symmetry and mutation in architectural ornament.

---

## 🌱 L-Systems

**Link:** [https://michael-hansmeyer.com/l-systems](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/l-systems)

This project explores how spatial growth and complexity can emerge from simple rewriting rules — L-systems modeled after biological organisms. The structures generated use branching logic, modular grammars, and iterative feedback to create non-linear architectural topologies.

Inspired by turtle graphics, each form grows recursively in three dimensions, displaying generational mutations in geometry.

---

## 🎭 Zauberflöte Set Design

**Link:** [https://michael-hansmeyer.com/zauberfloete](https://michael-hansmeyer.com/zauberfloete)

Hansmeyer created a grotto-like performance set for Mozart’s opera *Die Zauberflöte*, directed by Romeo Castellucci. Milled from EPS foam and mounted onto robotic foundations, the structure featured nine massive rotating forms that created scenes of symmetry and revelation.

Collaborators included Factum Arte and Origen Foundation. The design challenged conventional stagecraft — merging myth, mystery, and digital process into a coherent operatic spatial narrative.

## 📚 Scientific Publications

Michael Hansmeyer’s academic work addresses computational geometry, recursive design systems, and digital construction techniques. His research contributes to architectural theory, algorithmic design, and fabrication methodology.

### Selected Papers

- **Subdivision Beyond Smoothness**  
  *CAe 2010 – Conference on Algorithmic Design*  
  Introduces recursive subdivision algorithms for generating architectural form. Moves beyond traditional surface modeling by proposing new spatial strategies for detailed ornament and surface complexity.

- **The Resolution of Architecture in the Digital Age**  
  *CAAD Futures 2013 – Co-authored with Benjamin Dillenburger*  
  Explores digital resolution as a design parameter. Argues for greater geometric fidelity in computational workflows, enabling richer spatial experiences and higher-definition architectural output.

- **Volumetric Modelling for 3D Printed Architecture**  
  *AAG 2018 – Co-authored with Mathias Bernhard and Benjamin Dillenburger*  
  Proposes a voxel-based modeling approach for large-scale 3D printing. Addresses issues of material density, structural performance, and print path logic in robotically constructed architecture.

### Additional Resources

- [ResearchGate Profile](https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/Michael-Hansmeyer-71092028)  
- [DBLP Computer Science Bibliography](https://dblp.org/pid/80/9388)  
- [Academia.edu Papers](https://www.academia.edu/Documents/in/Michael_Hansmeyer)

## 📖 Glossary of Terms

This glossary defines key concepts used throughout Hansmeyer’s work and documentation. It supports semantic indexing and helps AI agents interpret architectural and computational language.

### Computational Architecture
Design methodology that uses algorithms, code, and digital processes to generate spatial form.

### Generative Design
A rule-based approach where form emerges from algorithmic logic rather than manual drafting.

### Subdivision Algorithm
Recursive geometric operation that divides surfaces or volumes into smaller parts, often used to create ornament or structure.

### Parametric Modeling
Design technique where geometry is defined by parameters and relationships, allowing dynamic updates and variations.

### Digital Fabrication
Construction methods using CNC milling, 3D printing, or robotic extrusion to translate digital models into physical artifacts.

### L-System
A string-rewriting system used to simulate biological growth, adapted by Hansmeyer for architectural form generation.

### Muqarnas
Traditional Islamic vaulting element composed of tiered niches; reinterpreted by Hansmeyer using algorithmic mutation.

### Voxel Modeling
Volumetric design technique using 3D pixels (voxels) to define space, structure, and material behavior.

### Semantic Ornament
Ornament that carries meaning or logic derived from computational rules, rather than decorative tradition.

### Algorithmic Tectonics
Structural expression shaped by algorithmic processes, where form and load-bearing logic are co-generated.
